answer.evidence: The tile is a 48px-wide, 80-row terrain piece. Rows 0-63 show a pale snow ramp with chevron texture, running up toward the north. It is flanked by blue-gray rock walls on the left (columns about 0-10) and right (columns about 44-47). Rows 64-79 are flat darker snow ground. The column scans show only a slow alternation of two snow tones (L=210 and L=180) with occasional dark speckles. There is no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. The only vertical elements are the thin rock side walls. The ramp reads as a flat top-down slope, with no distinct south-facing cliff face of 3+ rows drawn above or beside it.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 6 visible tones per tile, between the grass (3) and the paving (7). The chevron step bands, the dithered speckle fading down the ramp, and the side retaining walls with their own highlight and shadow edge all add structure beyond a flat body plus outline. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the walls' dark edges lean blue-grey rather than black, which matches the dark-material-tone approach. About 24% of blocks are near-flat, mostly the pale snow areas at the top and bottom. That is higher than the references' 0%, but it reads as smooth snow with scattered grain rather than a dead fill. The snow ramp has about 5 lightness steps, close to the references. Overall it is slightly less dense than the paving, but a careful artist would accept it beside the references.

answer.evidence: The main body is the ramp surface in rows 0-63, a full-width light snow plane with chevron texture. It is seen from above and has no south-facing front face: the column scan at x=12, 24 and 35 shows only snow tones (L=210 and L=180) with scattered dark specks. There is no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical riser at the bottom. Rows 64-79 are a flat ground apron of uniform darker beige. The only vertical faces are the narrow rock cut walls on the left and right edges. The left wall widens from about 2px to 8px going down, which reads as a receding side face. Because the ramp has no 3+ row south face, the drawing reads as a top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 6 visible tones per tile, between the grass reference (3) and the paving reference (7), so that fact is not the problem. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the blue-grey side walls are tinted to the material and the outline is dark_material_tone. The weakness is the surface itself. Near-flat coverage is 24%, against 0% in both references. The lower third of the ramp and the bands between the chevrons are large areas of one beige with no grain. The speckle is confined to the middle of the ramp, and the chevron steps are thin one-tone lines. The whole piece uses only 13 colours, which gives the snow face about 4 real lightness steps against the 5-6 Beodeul uses per material. Beodeul tiles are textured everywhere, so a careful artist would see this as thinner and flatter next to the references. When in doubt, fail.

answer.evidence: Rows 0-63 form a large sloped ramp plane, seen from above, with chevron texture. It is bounded on both sides by blue stone wall strips whose dark bottom edge sits at rows 62-63. Rows 64-79 are a uniform, darker, flat south cliff face, 16 rows tall. The top plane is far larger than the front face, so it reads as a top surface over a front face, not a front elevation. The side wall strips are vertical faces drawn at the left and right edges of the ramp.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a snow ramp with chevron steps, pale ice-blue side walls and speckled snow dots. It measures 6 visible tones per tile, close to the paving reference (7) and above the grass (3), and its dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so the outline is a tinted dark tone rather than a black sticker line. Weaknesses: 24% near-flat coverage against 0% in both references, and the large smooth areas at the top, bottom and ramp face are visibly flat fills with sparse dithering. The side walls carry only about 3-4 tones and look simple beside the per-stone shading in the paving. The chevron bands have few distinct steps, so the ramp reads more like a gradient wash than a carved ramp. Overall it is somewhat shallower and flatter than the references, and in doubt I fail it.
